newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish nuclear power phase-out cost disclosed.
newsitem.headline: Swedish nuclear power phase-out cost disclosed.

text.p: An energy deal agreed this week to phase out nuclear power in Sweden will cost the state about nine billion crowns ($1.2 billion) over a seven-year period, a government statement said on Tuesday.

The Industry and Trade Department said the agreement between the ruling Social Democrats, Centre and Left parties, involved the closure of a nuclear reactor at Barseback on Sweden's west coast by July 1998 before an autumn election.
It also involved the closure of one more of Sweden's 12 nuclear power stations by July 1, 2001.
"The programme will be fully financed," the statement said. "The parties behind the agreement will agree on suitable financing."
No further details about financing were released.
The statement said negotiations had begun with the owner of Barseback, Sydkraft which is Sweden's largest independent energy supplier.
The Industry and Trade Department said state-owned power company Vattenfall would actively cooperate on the changes in the energy system and a central energy authority would be created.
The agreement, reported reached last weekend, prompted market concern over how the closure process would be funded.
It pushed debt yields up on Monday as the crown weakened.

The department said the agreement was also designed to encourage both private and commercial enterprises to look at using alternative sources of power. It would bring in new ways of producing electricity in coming years.
"The result of the energy agreement and the closure of Barseback lays the foundations for further decisions on the continuing adjustment," the statement said.
"The decision over the continuing phase out will be made before the end of the next mandate period (in 2002)."
The agreement between the three parties, which hold 210 of the 349 seats in Sweden's parliament, ended a 17-year-old deadlock on the nation's nuclear industry.
Industry Minister Anders Sundstrom, who is responsible for energy, has described the agreement as "very responsible".
"It concerns how a nuclear power phase out will begin and it meets demands that the industry will not be hurt. It will give increased employment," Sundstrom said.
A plan to phase out the country's nuclear programme has been in the air since a national referendum in 1980 when Swedes voted to gradually phase out nuclear power.
Parliament eventually set the year 2010 as the target for making Sweden nuclear-free.

Critics of the plan, particularly from energy-intensive industries, say Sweden has not made alternative arrangements for electricity supply. Nuclear power currently meets half the country's electricity needs.

A proposal to replace the two reactors with natural gas or oil could go against a 1993 parliamentary ruling that by 2000 carbon dioxide emissions should not exceed 1990 levels and that should decline after 2000. ($ = 7.276 Swedish Crowns)
